clue.text: Nobody wants to prevent him having his fling

definitions.text: Nobody wants to prevent him having his fling

parts.words: Nobody wants to prevent him having his fling
parts.note: the fling is the famous Scottish dance named after the hill country of the north, so nobody begrudges a man from there his dance

explanation.surface: A carefree fellow whose wild escapades everyone indulges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' reads as a romantic fling or a spree; here it is the Highland fling, a vigorous solo Scottish dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Scottish uplands is the natural performer of the dance that bears his region's name.

clue.text: Liquor goes to their heads

parts.note: a ... is a large cask for beer or wine, so drink goes into the heads of these farm animals

explanation.surface: Drink makes them giddy.
explanation.walkthrough: A hogshead is a large barrel; read it as the heads of pigs into which the liquor goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs are swine, and a barrel for ale is named for their heads.

clue.text: These shrubs come up first class in cultivated areas

indicators.note: the reversed rating is placed inside the word for cultivated areas

parts.note: gardens are cultivated areas

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: A1 means first class

explanation.surface: Shrubs that thrive best in tended plots.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, the old Lloyd's Register mark for a first-rate ship, means first class; 'come up' turns it over in this down entry before it is planted in the beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardenias are evergreen bushes with fragrant white blooms.

clue.text: Landed in Scotland with a bonnet, perhaps

definitions.text: Landed in Scotland with a bonnet, perhaps

parts.words: Landed in Scotland with a bonnet, perhaps
parts.note: landed means owning land, and a Scottish landowner might wear a bonnet, the Scots word for a cap

explanation.surface: Arrived north of the border wearing a cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Landed' looks like arrived; it is the adjective, owning an estate. A Scottish bonnet is a soft cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is the owner of a Scottish estate.

clue.text: Threadbare condition of a wideawake hat ?

definitions.text: Threadbare condition of a wideawake hat ?

parts.words: Threadbare condition of a wideawake hat
parts.note: a wideawake is a broad-brimmed felt hat; worn fabric has lost its raised pile, and someone wide awake has had no snooze

explanation.surface: A shabby old felt hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A wideawake is a soft broad-brimmed felt hat. Nap is both the raised pile on cloth and a short sleep, which the wide-awake lack.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth worn smooth has lost its pile, and a person wide awake has had no doze.

clue.text: He makes one cross at times

definitions.text: He makes one cross at times

parts.words: He makes one cross at times
parts.note: a cross is the mark put on a ballot paper, made at the times of polls

explanation.surface: A man who now and then annoys people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes one cross' reads as angers someone; it is putting a single X on a ballot paper at elections.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter marks a ballot paper with an X at each poll.

clue.text: In truth she goes to the City.

indicators.note: she going off to the City means that word departs from the longer word, leaving the girl behind

parts.note: veracity means truthfulness
the City is London's financial district, written here as the plain word city

explanation.surface: Honestly, the woman is off up to town.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says a girl's name followed by CITY makes a word for truth: take CITY away from VERACITY and the girl remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Vera is a woman's given name, so 'she' stands for her.

clue.text: A supporter of the Board of Education.

definitions.text: A supporter of the Board of Education.

parts.words: A supporter of the Board of Education
parts.note: the Board of Education was a government department, but here the board is a classroom blackboard and the supporter is its stand

explanation.surface: A backer of the government's schools department.
explanation.walkthrough: The Board of Education was the old English ministry for schools; here the board is a classroom blackboard, and the supporter is the frame it rests on.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden stand holds a blackboard or canvas upright.

clue.text: He may be quite modern — even if Victorian?

definitions.text: He may be quite modern — even if Victorian?

parts.words: He may be quite modern — even if Victorian
parts.note: Victorian looks like belonging to the nineteenth century, but it also means from the state of Victoria

explanation.surface: Someone up to date despite old-fashioned roots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victorian' suggests the 1800s; a person from the state of Victoria, Melbourne's state, is a present-day citizen of that country.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria is a state of that nation, so a Victorian is one of its citizens.

clue.text: Return to digs for economy's sake ?

definitions.text: Return to digs for economy's sake ?

parts.words: Return to digs for economy's sake
parts.note: digs looks like lodgings, but read as digging again, a second trench; cutting back spending shares the word

explanation.surface: Moving back to cheap lodgings to save money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' is British slang for rented lodgings; here it means digging, so returning to it is to trench again.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrench is to cut back spending, and literally it is to dig a fresh earthwork.

clue.text: Writer had a maxim

parts.note: a maxim looks like a wise saying, but Maxim was the first name of this Russian novelist

explanation.surface: An author lived by a guiding motto.
explanation.walkthrough: The Russian writer was Maxim Gorki (Gorky), author of 'The Lower Depths'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian novelist and playwright Alexei Peshkov wrote under the pen name Maxim Gorki.

clue.text: Ladies of high standing but narrow outlook ?

definitions.text: Ladies of high standing but narrow outlook ?

parts.words: Ladies of high standing but narrow outlook
parts.note: titled noblewomen, read also as women who peer, that is, look with narrowed eyes

explanation.surface: Aristocratic women who are snobbishly small-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Narrow outlook' sounds like bigotry; it is the act of peering, squinting closely, so the noblewomen are also 'peer-esses'.
explanation.definitionFit: Women holding a title in the nobility, as a duchess or countess does, are of high social rank.

clue.text: Quite overcome by the rhythm of the Danse Macabre ?

definitions.text: the rhythm of the Danse Macabre
definitions.meaning: the Danse Macabre is the dance of the dead, so its rhythm is a beat for corpses

explanation.surface: Exhausted after keeping time to Saint-Saens's ghoulish dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Danse Macabre is the medieval 'dance of death' in which skeletons dance, also a piece by Saint-Saens.
explanation.definitionFit: Being totally exhausted is being worn out; a pulse kept by skeletons dancing would be a beat of the dead.

clue.text: He should have a direct approach to government

definitions.text: He should have a direct approach to government

parts.words: He should have a direct approach to government
parts.note: a sovereign who governs, and also a straight-edged measuring stick, which is literally direct

explanation.surface: A head of state ought to govern in a straightforward way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' suggests forthright politics; it is also the straightness of the drawing instrument with the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch governs a country, and a straightedge for drawing lines shares the name.

clue.text: Holiday approval for desert island service

parts.note: saying 'good' expresses approval
Man Friday served Robinson Crusoe on his desert island

explanation.surface: Taking a holiday to attend a castaway's church service.
explanation.walkthrough: Friday is Crusoe's servant in Defoe's novel, so he stands for 'desert island service'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Friday before Easter is a public holiday in many countries.

clue.text: A poet is quite likely to induce sleep

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for drugs that do this, the answer being a plural noun

indicators.note: what is quite likely is only probable, so the letters may well fall in some other order

explanation.surface: A dig at poets whose verse sends readers off to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite likely' tells you to rearrange A POET IS. The definition is loose: the answer names drugs that induce sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Opium-derived drugs such as morphine are narcotics that bring on drowsiness.

clue.text: They travel behind, but show what's coming

definitions.meaning: vehicles towed behind a car or lorry

explanation.surface: People lagging at the back who still foretell the future.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses share one word: towed vehicles, and cinema previews.
explanation.definitionFit: Towed wagons follow a car, and short film previews advertise future releases.

clue.text: Oxford College in genuine restoration

indicators.note: the college sits within the word for genuine

parts.note: genuine means real
New College is one of the colleges of Oxford University

explanation.surface: An Oxford college gets a proper refurbishment.
explanation.walkthrough: New College is one of Oxford's colleges despite dating from 1379; it sits inside the word for genuine.
explanation.definitionFit: Restoring something is a renovation, making it fresh again.

clue.text: Not a game for sea-horses

parts.note: the sport is like polo played in a pool, with swimmers rather than mounted riders, so sea-horses are not needed

explanation.surface: A pastime unsuited to marine creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: Polo is played on horseback; its pool version has no horses at all, of sea or land.
explanation.definitionFit: Swimmers play this ball game in a pool, in teams of seven.

clue.text: Aspired, in a way, to helplessness

indicators.note: a way can be a manner of arranging, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone who aimed high and ended up powerless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' tells you to rearrange ASPIRED.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter hopelessness is the feeling of being unable to help oneself.

clue.text: "There's the —— That makes calamity of so long life" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: There's the —— That makes calamity of so long life

parts.words: There's the —— That makes calamity of so long life
parts.note: a line from Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech with one word blanked, meaning consideration

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet's soliloquy with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Hamlet's line 'There's the respect / That makes calamity of so long life'; respect here means consideration.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's line the missing word means the consideration that keeps people enduring hardship.

clue.text: About headgear Mother can be adept

indicators.note: Mother goes about, that is around, the headgear

parts.note: mama is a word for mother
a hat is headgear

explanation.surface: Mum fussing over a hat proves she has hidden expertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' means the doubled form of Mother wraps around the headgear. An adept is a person skilled in esoteric arts, as a Hindu sage is held to be.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mahatma is a revered sage credited with special wisdom, like a master initiate.

clue.text: A letter in Greek leads to his total confusion

parts.words: A letter in Greek leads to
parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, and it leads, coming first

indicators.note: confusion throws the letters of total into disorder

explanation.surface: A single Greek letter throws someone into a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: MU is followed by the anagram LATTO, from 'confusion' acting on TOTAL. The definition is just 'his', the person meant, an old-fashioned style.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for the person of mixed parentage whom the clue refers to.

clue.text: Get knotted, composer !

explanation.surface: A rude dismissal shouted at a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted' is British slang for 'go away'; here it is the plain sense, to become tangled.
explanation.definitionFit: Threads that tangle form snarls, and the French musician wrote Bolero.

clue.text: He may show his hand.

parts.note: showing one's hand sounds like revealing intentions in cards, but a show of hands is a vote

explanation.surface: A card player who may reveal what he holds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show his hand' suggests cards; it is raising a hand in a show of hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone casting a ballot may do so by raising a hand.

clue.text: Lone Royalist disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed letters are knocked out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A lone supporter of the crown is troubled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' tells you to rearrange ROYALIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Lone means single, by oneself.

clue.text: See this on the boil

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'See this on the boil' (5) as printed on the scan gives THING by no parse I can find; 'See' and 'on the boil' do not yield it, and no search or reprint was available.

clue.text: Eddy changed colour .

indicators.note: the name is changed, its letters rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A boy called Eddy dyed his hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges EDDY; the whole clue then describes the result, something that changed colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Something coloured with a stain has had its hue altered.

clue.text: Just the thing to prevent a split?

parts.note: to deter is to prevent or discourage
a rent is a split or tear

explanation.surface: A remedy that stops a tear from forming.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue also reads as a whole: the deterrent is 'the thing to prevent a split'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deterrent is the very means of discouraging something, the fitting measure for the job.

clue.text: But it wasn't used in building the White Tower

definitions.text: But it wasn't used in building the White Tower

parts.words: But it wasn't used in building the White Tower
parts.note: the White Tower is the keep of the Tower of London, built of stone, not of the white tusk material of the idealist's proverbial tower

explanation.surface: A remark on the stone of the Tower of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Tower is the central keep of the Tower of London; an 'ivory tower' is a place of unworldly retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tusk material is white, yet the famous white keep was built of stone, unlike the tower of academic seclusion.

clue.text: The right distance in which to back a vehicle

indicators.note: to back is to reverse, so the vehicle's name is read backwards

parts.note: a dray is a low cart, as used by brewers

explanation.surface: Advice on how much room is needed for reversing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to back' turns DRAY round. A yard is also an enclosure where one might back a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: The yard is a unit of length of three feet.

clue.text: Fortress soundly held by Agrippa ?

definitions.meaning: Agrippa is read as 'a gripper', whose grip is a firm hold

explanation.surface: A Roman general's citadel held securely.
explanation.walkthrough: Agrippa was a Roman general; the name is split as 'a grip', and a strong grip is a firm hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified place is a citadel, and a firm grasp is a powerful grip.
